entries.name: pair_spec_side_startswith_lie_ls-errored#0
entries.script: [P1] `Coll[Byte] CONSTANT .zip(Coll(0,1,2))` — a `PairOfCols` whose **ls is specialised** (`zip` keeps both sides as they are, `CollsOverArrays.scala:42`) — `.startsWith(ys)` where `ys` is a pair collection whose own ls is declared `Coll[Byte]` and evaluates to `Coll[Long]`. `PairOfCols.startsWith` (`:398-406`) DELEGATES to `ls.startsWith(yp.ls)`, so the specialised side's array cast fires: `ClassCastException`. **SEPARATING, and the row that distinguishes pair collections from the A-family:** `getOrElse`/`updated` on a pair cast the whole default to `Tuple2` first and are blind to the sides' classes, but startsWith/endsWith are not.

entries.name: pair_gen_side_startswith_lie_ls-accept#1
entries.script: [P2] The same with a GENERIC ls (a ConcreteCollection of the same bytes): returns **`true`** at cost 190 — the delegated `startsWith` compares boxed elements and `1L == 1`, exactly as in the flat S2 row. The pair's rs is identical on both sides, so the only difference is the ls's runtime class.

entries.name: pair_spec_side_startswith_wellformed-accept#2
entries.script: [P3] **CONTROL:** the specialised-ls receiver with a well-typed pair argument returns `true` at cost 155.

entries.name: pair_gen_side_startswith_wellformed-accept#3
entries.script: [P4] **CONTROL:** the generic-ls receiver, same argument, `true` at cost 185.

entries.name: pair_spec_side_endswith_lie_ls-errored#4
entries.script: [P5] `endsWith` on the same pair receiver: the same delegation, the same cast. **SEPARATING.**

entries.name: pair_gen_side_endswith_lie_ls-accept#5
entries.script: [P6] Its generic twin returns **`false`** at cost 190 — the same argument that made P2 `true`, because `(1,2,3)` does not END with `1L`. The P2/P6 asymmetry pins the comparison as numeric rather than refused, inside a pair.

entries.name: startswith_pair_empty_primitive_arg-errored#6
entries.script: [P7] `Coll[(Int,Int)]` CONSTANT — a `PairOfCols` — `.startsWith(ys)` where `ys` is declared `Coll[(Int,Int)]` and evaluates to an EMPTY `Coll[Int]`. With a NON-pair argument the side-by-side delegation is unavailable and the fallback casts the argument's array, so this throws `ClassCastException` BEFORE any length test. **An empty argument is not a free pass:** the array is cast, not read. **SEPARATING:** an implementation that holds a pair collection as two columns, or that tests the argument's LENGTH before its class, answers `true` here — an over-accept of a comparison the JVM refuses.

entries.name: startswith_pair_nonempty_primitive_arg-errored#7
entries.script: [P8] The same with ONE Int in the argument: the same `ClassCastException`. It is what says P7 is about the array's class and not about an empty-prefix shortcut. **SEPARATING**, and the row an implementation that compares element-wise answers `false` on.

entries.name: startswith_pair_specialised_byte_arg-errored#8
entries.script: [P9] The same with a `Coll[Byte]` CONSTANT argument — the deserializer's specialised `$mcB$sp` over `[B` (`CoreDataSerializer.scala:174`): also `ClassCastException`. Any primitive backing does it, and the argument's own specialisation adds nothing. **SEPARATING.**

entries.name: startswith_pair_empty_reference_arg-accept#9
entries.script: [P10] The REFERENCE-array half: an argument declared `Coll[(Int,Int)]` that evaluates to an EMPTY `Coll[Coll[Int]]` is ACCEPTED and answers **`true`** at cost 55 — a `[Lsigma/Coll;` casts to `[Ljava/lang/Object;`, and an empty prefix is a prefix. **The P7/P10 pair is the row to read:** same receiver, same call, both arguments EMPTY, and the verdict turns on whether the argument's array is primitive.

entries.name: startswith_pair_nonempty_reference_arg-accept#10
entries.script: [P11] One `Coll[Int]` in that argument and the answer is **`false`** at cost 80: the cast succeeds and the comparison then fails on the element, a `Coll` being no `Tuple2`. The bound on P10 — the reference argument is answered, not waved through.

entries.name: endswith_pair_empty_primitive_arg-errored#11
entries.script: [P12] `endsWith` takes the identical path (`:405`) and throws on the empty primitive argument too. **SEPARATING**, and it doubles P7 on the other end of the collection.

entries.name: endswith_pair_empty_reference_arg-accept#12
entries.script: [P13] **CONTROL:** `endsWith` with the empty REFERENCE argument answers `true` at cost 55, the mirror of P10 — so P12 is the argument's array and not the end chosen.

entries.name: startswith_pair_prefix_arg_control-accept#13
entries.script: [P14] **CONTROL:** an honest pair-collection prefix `Coll((1,2))` answers `true` at cost 65 through the side-by-side delegation P1-P6 exercise. It is what shows P7-P9 are about the argument's KIND and not about the receiver.

entries.name: startswith_pair_empty_pair_arg_control-accept#14
entries.script: [P15] **CONTROL:** an EMPTY pair argument answers `true` at cost 40 — the delegated path has its own empty case, so emptiness is fatal only when the argument is a non-pair over a primitive array.

entries.name: mapped_receiver_empty_primitive_arg-accept#15
entries.script: [P16] **THE PAIR SHAPE DECIDES IT, NOT THE ITEM TYPE:** `pairConst.map(x => x)` is a plain `CollOverArray` over `[Lscala.Tuple2;` (family I), and the SAME empty primitive argument now answers **`true`** at cost 105 where P7 throws. One identity `map` on the RECEIVER flips the verdict — the fourth operation the pair shape decides, after `getOrElse`, `ByIndex` and the item-typed stores, and the one where the argument is what gets cast.
